lessons.title: What Is a Financial Crisis? Banking, Currency, and Debt Crises Explained

body.text: Every financial crisis, from 1929 to today, is a failure of one of three promises: a bank promising your money back, a country promising its currency holds value, or a government promising to repay its debt.

children.text: On 5 March 2020, customers of Yes Bank woke up to a message no Indian depositor wants to read. The RBI had placed the bank under a moratorium, and withdrawals were capped at ₹50,000 per depositor. ATM queues formed across Mumbai within hours. The bank was rescued in 13 days, but for those two weeks, millions of people learnt what a broken banking promise feels like.
This course walks through a century of financial crises, in order. Before the timeline starts, you need a clear way to sort them. That is this lesson.
What Actually Counts as a Financial Crisis

A market falling 10% is not a crisis. A single company going bust is not a crisis. A financial crisis is when a core part of the financial system stops doing its job, and the damage spreads well beyond the people who made the original mistake. Economists call this kind of damage
systemic

markDefs.definition: Affecting the financial system as a whole, not just one institution or investor. A systemic problem spreads to people who had no direct exposure to its cause.

children.text: The IMF keeps the most widely used database of these events. Its researchers, Luc Laeven and Fabián Valencia, counted 151 systemic banking crises around the world between 1970 and 2017. Crises are not rare accidents. They are a recurring feature of how money works.

children.text: The Three Families of Financial Crisis
Almost every crisis in this course fits into one of three families, or a combination of them. Learn these three and every later lesson becomes easier to follow.

body.caption: The three families at a glance

The currency will hold its value against the dollar
Forex reserves falling fast, large current account deficit
The government will repay its borrowings
Debt rising faster than the economy, borrowing costs spiking

children.text: 1. Banking Crisis: When the Bank Cannot Pay You Back

A bank runs on a simple mismatch. Your savings account deposit can be withdrawn any day, but the bank has lent most of that money out as home loans and business loans that will only be repaid over years. This works perfectly as long as depositors do not all ask for their money at once.
When they do, that is a
bank run
. Here is how it breaks a bank, in round numbers.

markDefs.definition: A rush of depositors withdrawing money at the same time because they fear the bank will fail. A run can bring down even a healthy bank, because no bank keeps enough cash for everyone at once.

body.caption: A simplified bank facing a run (₹ crore)

cells: Cash and liquid assets on hand

children.text: On a normal day, ₹2 crore of withdrawals is easily met from ₹15 crore of cash. On the day of the run, depositors want ₹20 crore. The bank is ₹5 crore short. To raise it, it must sell loans in a hurry, and buyers of distressed loans always demand a discount. Every rupee of loans sold below its value eats into the bank's capital, which makes the next wave of depositors even more nervous.

body.title: Illiquid vs Insolvent: the distinction every crisis turns on

columns.label: Illiquid bank
points: Its loans are good and will be repaid over time
Can be saved by a central bank lending it cash against its assets

columns.label: Insolvent bank
points: Its loans have gone bad, so assets are worth less than deposits
Even with time, it cannot repay everyone
Needs fresh capital, a merger, or closure

body.title: The Cost of a Fire Sale
body.prompt: The bank in the table above is ₹5 crore short. In the panic, buyers will only pay 80% of the book value of its loans. What book value of loans (in ₹ crore) must the bank sell to raise exactly ₹5 crore of cash?
body.explanation: Cash raised = book value × 80%. So book value = ₹5 crore ÷ 0.80 = ₹6.25 crore. The bank gives up ₹6.25 crore of loans to get ₹5 crore of cash, a ₹1.25 crore loss straight out of its capital. This is how a liquidity problem turns into a solvency problem.

body.label: Your Safety Net in India
body.context: Deposit insurance from DICGC, a wholly owned RBI subsidiary, covers savings, current and fixed deposits up to ₹5 lakh (principal plus interest) in each bank. The limit was raised from ₹1 lakh in February 2020.

children.text: 2. Currency Crisis: When Money Suddenly Buys Less

A currency crisis is a sharp, sudden fall in a country's currency, usually because foreign investors pull money out faster than the central bank can defend the exchange rate. The central bank fights back by selling dollars from its
foreign exchange reserves
. When those reserves start running low, markets smell blood and the selling speeds up.

markDefs.definition: The stock of foreign currency (mostly US dollars), gold and other foreign assets held by a central bank. The RBI uses them to pay for essential imports and to steady the rupee.

children.text: India lived through a mild version in 2013. When the US Federal Reserve hinted in May that it would slow its bond buying, foreign investors began pulling money out of emerging markets. The rupee went from about ₹55 per dollar in May to a record low of ₹68.85 on 28 August 2013. Chapter 4 covers this episode in full.

body.title: What a Weak Rupee Does to an Importer
body.question: An Indian oil marketing company must pay $1 million for a crude cargo. The rupee moves from ₹55 to ₹68.85 per dollar before payment. Roughly how much more does the cargo cost in rupees?
options: No change, the price is fixed in dollars
body.explanation: At ₹55, $1 million costs ₹5.5 crore. At ₹68.85, it costs ₹6.885 crore. The extra cost is ₹1.385 crore, about 25% more for the exact same oil. The price in dollars did not change, but the rupee bill did. This is why currency crises feed straight into inflation.

children.text: 3. Sovereign Debt Crisis: When a Government Cannot Repay
Governments borrow by issuing bonds. A
sovereign debt crisis
begins when lenders start doubting repayment. They demand higher interest rates, which makes the debt even harder to service, which raises doubts further.

markDefs.definition: A situation where a government cannot, or will not, repay its borrowings on the original terms. It usually ends in a default, a restructuring where lenders accept less, or a bailout from the IMF or other governments.

children.text: The most dangerous version is debt borrowed in a foreign currency. A government can always print its own currency, but it cannot print dollars. Our neighbour Sri Lanka learnt this in 2022. With dollar reserves nearly exhausted and fuel and medicine imports collapsing, it announced in April 2022 that it would suspend payments on its foreign debt, and in May it defaulted for the first time in its history.

body.title: Show me the math: why dollar debt turns deadly

children.text: Imagine a country, call it Country X, that owes $10 billion to foreign lenders. Its currency trades at 200 per dollar.

Not one extra dollar was borrowed. But after the currency falls from 200 to 360, the government needs 80% more of its own money to repay the same loan. A currency crisis has created a debt crisis. This exact chain shows up again and again in this course.

body.title: Name It
body.textWithBlank: When a government fails to make a scheduled payment on its borrowings, it is said to be in sovereign ___.
body.explanation: A sovereign default is when a government misses payments owed to its lenders. Sri Lanka in 2022 and Greece, which forced private bondholders to accept large losses in its 2012 restructuring, are two modern examples.

children.text: Why the Three Families Rarely Travel Alone
The three types feed each other, which is why the biggest crises in history are combinations. Economists call a banking crisis and currency crisis happening together a
twin crisis
. The IMF research above also found that currency and sovereign debt crises tend to coincide with, or follow, banking crises. Here is the typical chain, using Thailand in 1997 as the template:

markDefs.definition: A banking crisis and a currency crisis occurring at the same time, each making the other worse. Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea in 1997 are classic examples.

children.text: Thai banks and companies borrowed heavily in dollars because dollar interest rates were lower than baht rates.
Foreign investors grew nervous and pulled money out. The central bank burnt through its reserves defending the baht.
On 2 July 1997, Thailand gave up and let the baht float. It fell sharply.
Every dollar loan suddenly cost far more in baht. Companies defaulted and bank loans went bad, triggering a banking crisis.
The government had to rescue the banks and turned to the IMF for support. Contagion then spread to Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea.

body.text: Notice the villain in almost every chain: borrowing in a currency you cannot print, to fund assets that earn in a currency you can. Keep an eye out for this pattern in every lesson ahead.

body.title: Crisis or Not?
body.question: Was the March 2020 Yes Bank episode a systemic banking crisis?
options: Yes, because depositors could not withdraw their money freely
No, it was the failure of a single bank that was resolved before the damage spread across the system
Yes, because it happened during the COVID crash
No, because Yes Bank was a private bank, and only public sector banks can cause crises
body.explanation: Yes Bank was a serious bank failure, not a systemic crisis. The RBI and the government capped withdrawals, SBI led a consortium that injected capital, and the moratorium ended after 13 days. Other banks kept functioning normally. A systemic crisis is one where the whole system is under stress, as in the US in 2008. Private banks can absolutely cause crises, so the last option is wrong.

body.title: Diagnose the Crisis
body.scenario: A country pegs its currency to the US dollar. Over six months, its foreign exchange reserves fall from $40 billion to $8 billion. Its largest banks have borrowed heavily in dollars and lent the money to local real estate developers, who earn rent in local currency. The government's own debt is modest and mostly in local currency.
body.prompt: Which of the three crisis types is most immediately at risk, which is likely to follow, and which is least likely? Explain the chain.
body.modelAnswer: Most immediate: a currency crisis. Reserves have fallen 80% in six months, so the central bank will soon be unable to defend the peg. Likely to follow: a banking crisis. Once the currency is devalued, banks' dollar borrowings become far more expensive in local currency, while their real estate loans still earn only local currency. Their losses could wipe out their capital, making this a twin crisis. Least likely, at least at first: a sovereign debt crisis, since government debt is modest and in local currency, which the government can always repay by printing. The risk rises later if the government has to borrow heavily to rescue the banks.

cards.definition: Risk that a problem spreads across the whole financial system, not just the institution where it started.
Many depositors withdrawing money at once out of fear the bank will fail, which can make the fear come true.
Illiquid: good assets, not enough cash today. Insolvent: assets are worth less than what is owed.
Foreign currency and gold held by a central bank, used to pay for imports and defend the currency.
A government failing to make payments on its debt as promised.
A banking crisis and a currency crisis happening together and reinforcing each other.

body.title: Five-Minute Crisis Radar for India
steps: Check India's latest forex reserves in the RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement and note how many months of imports they cover
Look up the current rupee to dollar rate and compare it with a year ago
Find the gross NPA ratio of your own bank in its latest quarterly results on NSE or BSE
Confirm your deposits in any single bank are within the ₹5 lakh DICGC cover
Note India's latest current account deficit as a % of GDP from the RBI's quarterly release

body.description: The RBI's free data portal for forex reserves, exchange rates and banking statistics. Most of the numbers in the checklist above live here.

points: A financial crisis is systemic: a core part of the financial system stops working and the damage spreads beyond those who caused it
Banking crises break the promise to return deposits; currency crises break the promise of a stable currency; sovereign debt crises break the promise of government repayment
A bank can fail from a run even when its loans are sound, because illiquidity forces fire sales that create real losses
Debt borrowed in a foreign currency is the most common link that turns a currency crisis into a banking or debt crisis
The worst crises in history combine two or three types, and the timeline in this course will show that pattern repeating
